chunks: "My rule of thumb is that the outer layers are for components and short connections, and the inner layers are for the signals I want protected.

On the top and bottom I put everything that has to touch a part: pad fanouts, short point-to-point links, power pours, and things I want to be able to probe or tune, like test points and RF matching networks.
Anything that carries a lot of current gets wide copper on the outer layers where the heat can leave.
On the inner signal layers, between two planes, I put long runs and fast or noisy signals, like clocks and DDR lines.
Because they're a stripline with a plane on each side, the field stays inside the board, so there's less radiation and less pickup from outside, plus better ESD immunity.
The cost is vias to get there, and I can't probe them. I also keep adjacent signal layers orthogonal to each other, one horizontal and one vertical, to reduce broadside crosstalk.
And I keep a whole bus or a differential pair on the same layer, because the propagation speed is different on outer and inner layers, and I'd rather not create skew by changing layer types."
